opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the way I'd frame it is that coding is really the most general-purpose tool we have for acting on the world through a computer. If you think about what an agent needs to do to be genuinely useful, whether that's analyzing data, operating software, automating a workflow in finance or operations or research, almost all of that eventually bottoms out in some form of program. Code is the language computers natively understand. So an agent that's deeply competent at coding isn't just a software engineer. It's an agent that can build its own tools whenever it needs them.

There's also a very practical reason from a research perspective, which is that coding is one of the few domains where you get really clean feedback signals. You can run the code, run the tests, see whether it compiles, check whether the output matches what you expected. That makes it an incredibly good environment for reinforcement learning. A lot of what we learned from systems like AlphaGo was that when you have a reliable reward signal, you can push capabilities way past what you get from imitation alone. Code gives you something close to that in a domain that actually matters economically.

And what we've seen is that the skills you develop in coding transfer. To write good code for a nontrivial task, a model has to plan over long horizons, break a problem into pieces, keep track of a lot of context, recover from errors, and verify its own work. Those are exactly the capabilities you need for any kind of serious knowledge work. So when you get a model that can reliably navigate a large codebase and ship a working change, you've in some sense built the core of a general agent. Then extending it to other domains becomes more about giving it the right context and the right interfaces than inventing a fundamentally new capability.

So for us, coding isn't the end goal. It's the foundation, the place where you can most rapidly bootstrap toward something much more general, which is an agent that can do real work for people across the whole range of things they do on a computer.

r001.rationale: The response says coding competence makes an agent more than a software engineer and frames coding as a general-purpose capability.

r002.rationale: It describes code as a way to act through computers and build tools, but does not present code-based function calls as the expected way language models interact with almost any software.

r003.rationale: It mentions work across domains and says other domains need the right context and interfaces, but does not state that combining reasoning over disparate organizational information with code-based software action enables that generalization.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, coding isn't really a vertical for us, it's more like the substrate. When you look at what knowledge work actually is, most of it reduces to manipulating information through some kind of digital interface, and code is the most general interface to a computer that exists. If an agent can write and run code, it can talk to any API, process any file, automate any workflow. So an agent that's genuinely good at software engineering already has the primitives to do a lot of other things.

The second reason is more about how you train these systems. Coding is one of the few domains where you get a reasonably clear signal about whether you succeeded. Tests pass or they don't. The build compiles or it doesn't. That verifiability lets you do reinforcement learning at scale, where the model actually learns from trying things over long horizons rather than just imitating. And the skills you pick up that way, planning, decomposing a problem, recovering from errors, checking your own work, those aren't really coding skills. They're general agentic skills that happen to be learnable in code because the feedback loop is so tight.

And then there's the practical side. Software engineers are the earliest adopters and the most demanding users. They'll tell you immediately when the agent is wrong, and they'll push it to the edge of what it can do. If you can build something that engineers trust to work autonomously for hours in a real codebase, you've solved most of the hard problems around reliability, context, and tool use that you'd need for any other kind of long-running work. So we see coding as the place where you prove the system works, and then the capability generalizes outward from there.

r001.rationale: The response treats coding as a general computer capability and software engineering as a work domain where that capability is developed and tested.

r002.rationale: It says an agent that writes and runs code can talk to any API, process files, and automate workflows, presenting code as a broadly applicable way to interact with software.

r003.rationale: It connects manipulating information through digital interfaces with acting through code on APIs and workflows, then says the resulting agent skills generalize to other kinds of work.

astra-6.text:
I think coding is foundational because it gives a model a way to act, not just a way to answer questions. A lot of work happens through software, and code is a very general interface to that software. If you can write code, you can analyze data, run an experiment, interact with an API, or automate a workflow. So the usefulness extends well beyond producing software as the final product.

The other piece is that coding gives you a feedback loop. You can try something, execute it, see what failed, and revise your approach. That’s a really important setting for learning how to work through a problem over many steps, because you have evidence about whether you’re making progress.

Now, that doesn’t mean being good at coding automatically makes you good at every other kind of work. You still need to understand the domain and what success means. But it gives you both a tool for taking action and a setting for developing the ability to try, check, and correct. Those are useful foundations for much more general systems.

r001.rationale: It presents coding as a general way to take action through software and says its value extends beyond producing software as the final product.

r002.rationale: It calls code a general software interface and mentions APIs, but does not state that language models are expected to use code-based function calls to interact with almost any software.

r003.rationale: It describes taking actions and using feedback to revise, but does not connect reasoning over disparate organizational information with code-based software actions to enable operational generalization across work categories.

sol-6.1.text:
I think coding is foundational because it gives a model a way to act, not just a way to answer questions. If you can write and execute code, you can use tools, analyze data, run experiments, and interact with other software. So the usefulness of that capability extends well beyond producing software for a human engineer.

It’s also an environment where you can get concrete feedback. You try something, run it, see what breaks, and revise your approach. That loop is important: the system has to connect its reasoning to an outcome rather than just produce a plausible explanation.

That doesn’t mean being good at coding automatically makes a system good at everything else. But it gives you a foundation for building agents that can take a goal, do work toward it, check the result, and keep going. A lot of work outside software engineering has that same structure.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes coding as a general capability from producing software for a human engineer, and says the capability extends beyond software engineering.

r002.rationale: It says code can help a model use tools and interact with other software, but does not present code-based function calls as the expected way language models will interact with almost any software.

r003.rationale: It connects code execution and feedback to work across domains, but does not state that reasoning over disparate organizational information combined with acting on software through code enables operational generalization.
